item.title: Efficient simulation of variational quantum circuits: representation, accuracy and CPU/GPU allocation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Direct Pauli evolution via NumPy accelerates two-layer full LiH variational evaluations 3.45-fold over elementary-gate simulation, whereas an RTX PRO 6000 GPU yields roughly 30-fold speedup over an 18-thread Aer CPU baseline for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM in FP64.

Grade 0.437 · 3.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Vojtvech Novák, Radovan Revcka, Ondvrej Knebl, Ivan Zelinka

Figure

Per-call latency of four-layer spin VHA in FP64 versus qubit count, comparing elementary gate decomposition, direct Pauli updates, specialized commuting-block updates, and single-GPU acceleration across thread counts.

Asks

How should simulation representation, precision, and CPU/GPU resource allocation be jointly chosen to minimize the cost of repeated variational quantum circuit energy evaluations under accuracy and hardware constraints?

But

Evaluations assume fixed-parameter scalar energy calls, not full optimizer convergence trajectories; unobserved vectors outside candidate comparison subsets are not certified; MPS requires low entanglement.

Tools

Qiskit Aer and Statevector · Pennylane Lightning direct Pauli evolution · CUDA-Q GPU adapter · Matrix product states (MPS) · NumPy state updates

Abstract

Classical circuit simulation supports quantum software development and verification and provides a baseline for assessing quantum advantage. We compare gate-based statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution and matrix product states for molecular and spin Variational Hamiltonian Ansatze and hardware-efficient ansatze on CPU/GPU systems, varying width, depth, precision and resource allocation. In the tested implementations, direct Pauli evolution benefits complex molecular VHA, whereas GPUs accelerate wider spin and hardware efficient circuits. Matrix product state is useful when limited entanglement permits accurate compression; corrected CPU FP32 can meet the tested tolerance while costing more than FP64. Workload size, startup, worker memory and task-specific profiling can change the preferred allocation. Matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerate two-layer full LiH by 3.45-fold; the GPU gives approximately 30-fold acceleration over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM, both in FP64. We provide a procedure for choosing representation, precision and worker allocation jointly, comparing the cost of complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory and core constraints.

item.title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — t-GQCE maps lattice dynamics to noninteracting quasiparticles on classical CPUs coupled to finite embedding models on QPUs. Adding ghost orbitals suppresses artificial undamped oscillations, yielding double occupancy 0.100 at t=5 for weak quench at B=7 compared to DMFT value 0.104.

Grade 0.402 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Joshua Aftergood, Daniele Guerci, Jacob Brunton, Feng Zhang, Thomas Iadecola, Peter P. Orth, Cai-Zhuang Wang, Nicola Lanatà, Yong-Xin Yao

Figure

Double occupancy versus time for weak and strong interaction quenches in the Hubbard model, showing t-GQCE systematically matching nonequilibrium DMFT and suppressing B=1 oscillations as bath orbitals increase (B=3,5,7). Infidelities remain below 5×10−4.

Asks

Can quantum embedding theories be extended to simulate real-time nonequilibrium dynamics of correlated electron lattices on hybrid quantum-classical hardware without continuous bath overheads?

Before

Conventional time-dependent Gutzwiller approximation (B=1) produces artificial, undamped coherent oscillations of local observables after an interaction quench.

But

Embedding states propagated along classically precomputed Hamiltonian trajectories rather than fully self-consistent quantum-in-the-loop evolution; reaches 0.01 target accuracy only when hardware noise rates are scaled down to one third.

Tools

time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation · adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulation (AVQDS) · IBM quantum hardware (ibmq_quito) · trapped-ion noise models and Quantinuum H2-Emulator · orbital-basis rotation measurements with mirror-circuit mitigation

Abstract

Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. We present the time-dependent Gutzwiller quantum-classical embedding framework, t-GQCE, for generic multi-orbital lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below 5×10⁻⁴. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of 0.01 for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with 10⁵ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.

item.title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Generalizes pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution to state-dependent operations without approximation. Reaches up to 24× higher throughput than CUDA-Q on distance-3 topological memories with amplitude damping, and up to 83× higher throughput on 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements.

Grade 0.364 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Louis Follet, Paavai Pari, Isidor Schoch, Thien Nguyen, Justin G. Lietz, Daniel Lowell, Brucek Khailany, Krysta M. Svore, Dirk R. Englund, Taylor L. Patti

Figure

Throughput speedup of generalized PTSBE over CUDA-Q and Clifft as a function of non-Clifford gate fraction and total shots across surface codes, color codes, and 16-to-30-qubit random circuits.

Asks

Can pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution be extended to circuits with mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels without approximation?

Before

Original PTSBE required stochastic outcomes to be state-independent (mixtures of unitaries), excluding mid-circuit measurements and non-twirled amplitude damping.

But

Single-precision statevectors; limited by GPU memory for caching intermediate state branches (requires 8⋅2n bytes per cached state, e.g., 8 GiB per state at n=30 qubits).

Tools

generalized pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) · delayed inner product algorithm · GPU statevector simulator (CUDA-Q extension) · multinomial branching and cached state reuse

Abstract

Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.

item.title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth using homogeneous Z- and X-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs) plus Toffoli states, at the cost of exponential space and dirty ancillae.

Grade 0.361 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Christopher Kang, Alexander Cowtan, Adam Bene Watts, Guillaume Dauphinais, Benjamin Ide

Asks

How to formalize reaction depth and minimize it for fault-tolerant coherent Boolean logic using LDPC-compatible PPM gatesets?

But

Requires exponential space and leaves some qubits dirty; uncomputation in adder and multiplier requires a low number of heterogeneous PPMs.

Tools

reaction depth formalization · homogeneous Z- and X-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs) · Toffoli state injection · AutoAND circuits · LDPC code operations

Abstract

Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program. In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection. We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous Z- and X-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.

item.title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — In a Kitaev-chain quantum reservoir, protected Majorana edge modes yield retention scaling as τe∼eN/ξ, balanced by local write-read residue ℛloc∼τe−2. Interactions (U≠0) autonomously load bulk memory into edge parities via second-order Liouvillian coupling at the expense of retention.

Grade 0.360 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Zhi-Lei Zhang, Lianxiang Cui, C. P. Sun, Kohei Nakajima, Kazuyuki Aihara

Figure

Bulk-to-edge loading W and edge retention S across chemical potential μ/t and interaction U/t, accompanied by delayed-input memory function and temporal integration test R2 showing performance gains from including the endpoint parity Pend at long timescales τtar.

Asks

Can a physical system hosting protected topological information perform reservoir computation via its bulk dynamics while retaining processed information in its protected boundary modes?

But

Numerical reservoir task simulations performed at N=10, Δ=t, and tτ=1.5; analytic linear reservoir description strictly requires U=0; requires ensemble-averaged readout without mid-circuit back action.

Tools

One-dimensional Kitaev chain model · Majorana covariance space formulation · Liouvillian Dyson expansion · Echo-state property analysis

Abstract

Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

item.title: Environment-assisted imaginary time evolution in feedback-based quantum algorithms
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Formulating imaginary time evolution as an environment-induced quantum operation inside FALQON achieves ground-state preparation across arbitrary initial states where standard FALQON stalls, reaching success probability p=1 within roughly 1000 layers on MaxCut.

Grade 0.359 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · J. C. Bellizotti Souza, M. C. de Oliveira

Figure

Panels show the feedback parameter β, approximation ratio r, and ground-state success probability p versus layer count k across 30 random initial states, plus layer requirements for p≥0.5 across graph sizes n. CITE-FALQON reaches r=1 and p=1 smoothly, whereas FALQON plateaus below p=0.4.

Asks

Can dissipation-induced non-unitary dynamics improve the convergence and circuit depth of feedback-based quantum algorithms?

Before

Unitary ITE-FALQON required approximations or ancilla overhead on quantum hardware to apply non-unitary exponential suppression factors; standard FALQON stalled at r≈0.86 and p=0.35 on average by layer k=1500 in MaxCut simulations.

But

Numerical simulations up to circuit depth k=1500; interaction with the environment is modeled phenomenologically without physical reservoir engineering or realistic gate/thermal noise.

Tools

Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) · Operator-sum representation / quantum channels · Imaginary time evolution · Numerical state-vector/density-matrix simulation

Code. https://github.com/yuyln/data-cite-falqon

Abstract

The Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) prepares ground states without classical parameter optimization, but requires deep circuits and can stagnate away from the ground state as a consequence of barren plateaus and symmetry protection. In order to avoid stagnation, imaginary time evolution (ITE) layers can be incorporated into FALQON layers, enhancing FALQON convergence. However, applying a non-unitary ITE layer in a closed quantum system is not possible, and approximations must be made to use ITE on real hardware; using an open quantum system formulation to incorporate ITE into FALQON represents a better approach. We describe ITE as a quantum operation induced by an environment, and combine it with the FALQON feedback law. In simulations of a frustrated Ising chain (ANNNI) and of MaxCut, the resulting algorithm prepares the ground state starting from any initial state, where FALQON can fail, and needs fewer layers on average when the initial state is fixed for the two investigated problems. The CITE-FALQON advantage strongly depends on the system phase for the ANNNI chain, and on the graph weights for the MaxCut problem.

item.arxave:abstract: The Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) prepares ground states without classical parameter optimization, but requires deep circuits and can stagnate away from the ground state as a consequence of barren plateaus and symmetry protection. In order to avoid stagnation, imaginary time evolution (ITE) layers can be incorporated into FALQON layers, enhancing FALQON convergence. However, applying a non-unitary ITE layer in a closed quantum system is not possible, and approximations must be made to use ITE on real hardware; using an open quantum system formulation to incorporate ITE into FALQON represents a better approach. We describe ITE as a quantum operation induced by an environment, and combine it with the FALQON feedback law. In simulations of a frustrated Ising chain (ANNNI) and of MaxCut, the resulting algorithm prepares the ground state starting from any initial state, where FALQON can fail, and needs fewer layers on average when the initial state is fixed for the two investigated problems. The CITE-FALQON advantage strongly depends on the system phase for the ANNNI chain, and on the graph weights for the MaxCut problem.

item.title: Fe²⁺:forsterite Qubit System
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Simulated X and Z logic gates achieve >99.7% fidelity at 1.15 ns gate times in Fe2+:forsterite at temperatures up to 10 K. Natural tunnel splitting is Δ=0.19 K (4.040 GHz) under zero field.

Grade 0.348 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers” · Dishaanth S. Pillai, G. M. Wysin

Figure

Gate infidelity of X and Z gates as a function of decoherence rate at T=10 K, showing infidelity remains below 10−3 at predicted direct-process relaxation rates.

Asks

Can the intrinsic zero-field splitting of a non-Kramers Fe2+ ion in forsterite host coherent qubit operations robust against thermal decoherence up to 10 K?

Before

Prior non-Kramers Fe2+ qubits (Smoleński et al.) required deliberately engineered lattice-mismatch epitaxial strain in CdSe/ZnSe quantum dots to induce degeneracy, demonstrated only spin-state characterization and optical readout, and had no coherent gate-control mechanism.

But

Theoretical simulation only; spin-phonon coupling constant GE is unmeasured; Raman and Orbach relaxation rates omitted because prefactors CR and AO are unknown; readout methods require lower temperatures than 10 K.

Tools

spin Hamiltonian diagonalization · time-dependent master equation simulation · surface acoustic wave (SAW) strain driving · Qiskit cross-validation

Abstract

Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe²⁺:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.

item.title: A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Constructed a nonsecular Lindblad master equation satisfying time-reversal KMS detailed balance with a time-uniform microscopic trace-norm error bound supt≥0⁡‖ρmic(t)−ρK(t)‖1≤Cλ2. Stationary state reproduces the exact mean-force Gibbs state up to O(λ4).

Grade 0.337 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems” · Ji-Hui Pei, Jin-Fu Chen

Figure

Normalized trace-norm error Δρ/λ2 versus scaled time λ2t for secular, intermediate, and nonsecular regimes. Shows TR-KMS completion retains O(λ2) accuracy across all regimes, whereas Davies and Scandi-Alhambra equations fail to maintain second-order bounds.

Asks

Can a completely positive nonsecular quantum master equation preserve detailed balance while maintaining a time-uniform O(λ2) error bound relative to microscopic dynamics?

Before

Davies equation gave supt≥0⁡Δρ(t)=O(1) when the secular approximation fails; Scandi-Alhambra equation gave Δρ(t)=O[λ(1+t/τd)].

But

Finite-dimensional system, weak coupling λ, bath with fast-decaying correlations, and rapid mixing on relaxation timescale τd∼λ−2.

Tools

Redfield equation completion · Hamiltonian of mean force reference · TR-KMS detailed balance · Resonance matching of coherent and dissipative kernels · Perturbative error bounds

Abstract

An effective theory of open quantum systems should preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and remain accurate throughout relaxation. Meeting both requirements is particularly challenging in quantum many-body systems, where dense spectra can invalidate the secular approximation even at weak coupling. Here we construct a nonsecular quantum master equation that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. Under suitable conditions, we prove a time-uniform O(λ²) bound on the difference between the predicted and exact reduced density matrices, where λ is the system-bath coupling strength. Our construction completes the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance. In this approach, TR-KMS detailed balance is compatible with resonance matching, whereas its counterpart without time reversal is not. In a benchmark against the exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, our equation maintains O(λ²) accuracy across secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming the existing detailed-balance equations tested. These results provide a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation.
